name: PX33
hook: Japan's first four-wheel-drive passenger car was finished, tested and then switched off by a planning decision, and Mitsubishi waited almost forty years to build another.
story:
Picture a shipyard in Kobe, 1935. Among the hulls and cranes sits something odd. A big, open four-door tourer, standing tall on its wheels.

The army asked for it. They wanted a staff car that could leave the road behind. So all four wheels are driven, all the time. No Japanese saloon had done that before.

The engineers keep going. A second stage follows in 1936 with a military engine. A diesel is in the works too, Japan's first with direct injection. Four finished cars roll out.

Then the rules change. Not on a track, but in a ministry. In 1937 the government decides Mitsubishi's factories should build trucks and buses. Passenger cars can wait. The whole project is cancelled.

The idea sleeps for decades. Then, in the early eighties, Mitsubishi builds a small four-wheel-drive called the Pajero. It goes on to win in the desert.

And the old PX33? Mitsubishi now calls it the start of that line.
description: The PX33 was a four-door, open-top passenger car built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries for the Japanese military. It was commissioned in 1934, and Mitsubishi says the army's automobile school asked for it. It was the first Japanese-built saloon with full-time four-wheel drive. Four prototypes were completed, with petrol engines first and a 6.7-litre direct-injection diesel in development. In 1937 the government moved Mitsubishi's capacity to trucks and buses and cancelled the project. Mitsubishi traces its four-wheel-drive line, and the Pajero, back to it.
